title: Philip Neri
hook: the laughing saint of Rome, who wore his clothes inside out to stay humble

segments.voice: Yesterday, noche oscura: John of the Cross, writing love poems in a tiny cell. Your line was on a dark night.

A priest is walking through the streets of Rome with half his beard shaved off. Another day, tradition says, he goes out with his clothes on inside out. People stare. Some laugh. That's the point. This is Philip Neri, and Rome remembers him as the laughing saint. People came to him for confession and advice, and some hoped to meet a holy man. What they found, the stories say, might be a joke, a silly hat, or a book of funny stories read aloud with a perfectly straight face. Behind it all sat a serious question: how do you stay humble when people start calling you a saint?

He lived in Rome in the age of the reformations, when the Catholic Church was working to renew itself from the inside. He didn't lead armies of preachers or write a famous book. He talked with people and heard confessions. He gathered young men in a room to pray, read scripture, sing and talk about God, and the community that grew from those meetings came to be called the Oratory. Tradition says that when people began treating him as a living saint, he'd do something ridiculous on purpose, so they'd laugh at him instead of praising him. He wasn't mocking holiness. He was guarding it. The saying linked to him is today's line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. It echoes a proverb in the King James Bible: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones." And Paul, in his second letter to the Corinthians, says of giving: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." Seen this way, cheerfulness isn't a mood that shows up when life is easy. It's a strength you can lean on. A heart that can laugh at itself is harder to puff up, and harder to crush. And if you don't need to look impressive, your attention is free to go to other people. Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the proverb he echoes sits in the Bible Christians share.

Do one small, humbly silly thing, never at anyone else's expense: hum a tune badly, or read a line aloud in a ridiculous voice, and let yourself smile. Notice the little voice asking what people would think, and breathe until it gets a little smaller. If you pray, hold the proverb gently: a merry heart doeth good like a medicine. If not, rest in the lightness of not having to look impressive.
Philip Neri. A priest of Rome remembered as the laughing saint, who made himself look silly on purpose to stay humble, and who treated cheerfulness as a strength of the heart.
Your line: cheerfulness strengthens the heart. Even a saint can wear his clothes inside out. I'm glad you came.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Philip Neri as a saint, and the Oratory communities that look back to him still gather for prayer, scripture and music; stories of his humor are often retold on his feast day.

chat.says: Why would a saint shave half his beard and walk around Rome like that?
options: To stay humble: if people laughed at him, they'd stop praising him.
To mock church leaders who were far too serious in his day.
To shock crowds into coming to hear his long sermons.
